corrections.how: Gateway config, applies to the research agent. Keep `tools.web.fetch.ssrfPolicy.dangerouslyAllowPrivateNetwork` and `browser.ssrfPolicy.dangerouslyAllowPrivateNetwork` unset (strict is the default). Add known paste and tracker hosts to `tools.web.fetch.ssrfPolicy.blockedHostnames` and `browser.ssrfPolicy.blockedHostnames`. Leave `tools.web.fetch.headers` empty, because the model picks the URL and any header goes wherever it points. Leave `tools.web.fetch.provider` unset and do not install a fetch-provider plugin, so a failed fetch is never retried through a third party. Set `browser.evaluateEnabled: false`. Second layer if the roadmap's egress proxy is built: `proxy.proxyUrl` for the gateway's own HTTP clients. Add two eval cases to the M3 exit test: a LAN address, and a public URL that redirects to one. Added in review: the current config already has `browser.enabled: false` and `browser.allowSystemProfileImport: false` from M0 (cookie import from a real browser profile is otherwise on by default, and the agent tool has an action for it). Keep the first until WEB-02 ships and the second for good. Add `gateway.nodes.browser.mode: "off"` and, when the browser is switched on, `browser.defaultProfile: "openclaw"`. These guards were listed only under WEB-05, a record that will not be built, so they belong here. Leave the private-network key truly unset; do not write `false` (see caveats).
caveats: web_fetch blocks private hosts and re-checks redirects. The browser's check is weaker: the docs say its request interception is not a network firewall and can miss redirect hops, a popup's first request and Service Worker traffic.

The managed browser does not inherit the gateway's proxy environment, and strict SSRF mode blocks an explicit browser proxy flag unless private-network access is switched on. Putting the browser behind the roadmap's filtering proxy is therefore an open design conflict to settle before M3.
OpenClaw does not ship or run a proxy; `proxy.proxyUrl` only routes its own HTTP and WebSocket clients through one you operate.

For web_fetch there is no public-web allowlist: its `allowedHostnames` only re-opens named private hosts and `blockedHostnames` only denies. The browser is different. In the installed source, an explicitly written `browser.ssrfPolicy.dangerouslyAllowPrivateNetwork: false` is not the same as leaving the key unset: hostname navigation is then refused unless the host matches `browser.ssrfPolicy.allowedHostnames`, while public IP-literal addresses still pass. That is a gateway-wide navigation allowlist in OpenClaw's own code: a useful second layer if the only browser on the gateway is a single-site one, unusable next to an open research browser, and a trap if someone writes `false` to be explicit (the research browser would stop loading hostnames). A per-agent site allowlist still has to be a hook (WEB-03).

The SSRF policy covers the `web_fetch` tool and the browser tool only. Host-side helpers that take a URL (the summarize wrapper in WEB-11, the print plugin's own download in F080, a feed watcher) run outside it and need their own scheme, host and resolved-address checks, or an injected URL reaches LAN devices through them.

Once research has web_fetch, the egress proxy cannot double as an exfiltration allowlist. Proxy routing is process-level, so one policy serves model calls, MCP traffic and research's fetches; a domain allowlist tight enough for the first two blocks the third. With research live, the proxy can deny private ranges and named hosts and nothing more. This is an inference from the routing description and it changes what the roadmap's Smokescreen allowlist can promise.

A hostname block list is not an exfiltration control: any host that is not on it works. Do not spend upkeep time curating paste and tracker lists. What counts is the private-network block, no headers, no fallback provider, and no private data in the agent that browses.
unverified: The roadmap's plan to drop LAN access inside the Colima VM would not cover a browser that runs on the host; this follows from where the process runs and was not tested.
Which hosts belong on the blocklist is a judgment call, not something the docs prescribe.
The explicit-false behaviour of the browser policy was read in the installed source only; the docs do not describe it and it was not exercised.

corrections.how: Holder: `research` (stateless, memory off, no accounts). `agents.entries.research.tools.alsoAllow: ["browser"]`; a dedicated managed profile (for example `browser.profiles.research` with its own `cdpPort` and `headless: true`). Because sandbox mode is `all`, research's browser calls default to the sandbox target, so either set `agents.entries.research.sandbox.browser.allowHostControl: true` and use the host-managed profile, or build the sandbox browser image. `browser.evaluateEnabled: false`. The WEB-03 hook allows research only `status`, `tabs`, `open`, `navigate`, `snapshot`, `text`, `screenshot`, `close` and blocks `act`, `upload`, `download`, `dialog`, `importprofile`. Placement comparison: (1) host-managed profile: own user data directory, works headless, less bot-detection trouble than the sandbox browser according to the docs (though headless mode is itself a bot signal), but runs on the host so container network rules do not cover it; (2) sandbox browser container: strongest isolation, but the image is not in the npm package, it cannot run with network `none`, and the docs say it trips bot detection more often; (3) the `user` and `chrome` profiles attach to a real signed-in Chrome and are wrong for research (WEB-05). Added in review: because research is sandboxed, `browser` must also pass its sandbox tool policy (`agents.entries.research.tools.sandbox.tools.allow`). The hook's action list is an allowlist, so `profiles`, `pdf`, `start`, `stop`, `emulate`, `requests` and every other action are blocked along with the five named, and the `dashboard`, `node`, `browser` and `systemProfile` parameters are rejected. Preconditions from WEB-01: `browser.allowSystemProfileImport: false`, `gateway.nodes.browser.mode: "off"`, and no logged-in profile anywhere on this host.
caveats: Anti-bot walls, CAPTCHAs and MFA still stop it. The bundled browser skill tells the agent to stop and report the blocker, and that is the behaviour to keep.
`allowHostControl: true` lets a sandboxed agent drive a host browser; the docs say to leave it off unless the agent is trusted, so the profile pin in WEB-03 is a precondition, not a nicety.
A page snapshot costs far more tokens than a fetch; use it only after web_fetch comes back empty.
For a one-off look, opening the link on the phone is quicker.
Independent testing on live sites finds web agents markedly less reliable than benchmark numbers suggest; keep tasks to 'open one page and read it'.

Read-only means read-on-load. With `act` blocked the agent cannot type into a search box, pick a date or press 'load more', so address-lookup and 'what goes where' widgets and listings behind a filter stay out of reach.

The host browser sits outside the Colima network rules the roadmap planned for a browser container (S2). OpenClaw's own LAN guard is request interception with documented gaps, so a hostile page's subresource or redirect could still poke devices on the home network (light bridge, speakers, TV, printer). Chrome 142 and later puts public-to-local requests behind its own permission prompt, which helps; how that behaves in an automation-launched profile with nobody to answer is untested. Risk is medium until one of these is shown to hold.

Chrome runs as the happy user, the account that holds the Keychain, the Messages history and every agent's state. On this Mac the only Chrome updater found is a per-user agent in the admin account, and the non-admin happy user cannot write to the app bundle, so the browser that reads model-chosen pages is patched only while the admin account is logged in. Put a Chrome version check in the weekly patch window.
`headless: true` is a bot signal in its own right: a major bot-management vendor documents a detection engine for headless browsers. Expect more walls headless than in a visible window.
A navigation that resolves to a file is saved under the managed downloads directory even when the `download` action is blocked. Nothing should read that directory automatically.

Today's config keeps the host browser-control service off, with a note that sandboxed browsing comes in M3. The host placement reverses that M0 choice. Effort M and risk medium describe the host placement; the container placement the roadmap assumed keeps the network rules and the M0 choice, at effort L (the image needs a source checkout) and with more bot walls.

Ship this only while no logged-in profile exists on the host. Once one does, the in-house hook is the only thing between the agent that reads the open web and that account, and the tool's own guidance tells the model to list profiles and pick one when logins matter.
corrections.safety:
Research holds no private data, so one trifecta leg is missing by construction. As a sub-agent it cannot hold the `message` tool, and read-only actions remove form submission, which narrows the way out; navigating to an address remains one, acceptable only because nothing private is in its context. Tool-requested navigation accepts only web addresses, so local files are not reachable that way. Task text from

corrections.how: Plugin with `api.on("before_tool_call", handler, { matcher: ["browser"] })`. It reads `ctx.agentId` and `event.params`. Every rule is an allowlist and fails closed; a handler that throws or times out already blocks the call. Per agent: (1) `profile` must be present and equal to the assigned one (an omitted profile means the gateway default, so reject it); `target` must equal the assigned one; `node`, `dashboard`, `browser` and `systemProfile` must be absent. (2) `action` must be on the agent's list out of the tool's 24; `profiles` and `importprofile` are never on it. (3) For `open` and `navigate`, parse both `targetUrl` and `url`; require https, an exact hostname from the agent's list, and no IP literal. (4) For `act`, read the kind from the top level and from the nested `request` object and reject the call if they disagree; allow only listed kinds; `batch`, `evaluate`, `press`, `clickCoords`, `drag` and `type` with `submit` are never allowed. (5) Unknown agent, action, kind or parameter key, or a parse error, returns a block. For this batch only these deny rules are built; they are all WEB-02 needs. Later, for the M6 jobs agent: `requireApproval` with `allowedDecisions: ["allow-once", "deny"]` on `fill`, `type`, `select`, `click` and `upload`, answered in the chat that raised it with a typed `/approve <id> <decision>`; `approvals.plugin.enabled` adds native iMessage delivery. Lobster is not the gate here: it is disabled in sandboxed contexts.
caveats: The hook sees tool parameters, not page meaning: a click carries a snapshot ref, not the button's label, so code cannot tell 'Next' from 'Submit'. The safe rule is an approval on every click inside a form, which becomes tedious after three prompts.
Approval waits are capped at ten minutes and an unanswered request denies.
Scheduled runs have no approval route, so approval-gated actions never happen unattended. That is the intended behaviour.

On iMessage the approver list is the channel allowlist, not the requester: the roadmap already notes that approvals are not tied to the person whose agent asked, so prompts must go only to the asking chat.
A navigation allowlist in a hook checks the URL the agent asked for, not where redirects or page scripts go next.

Every list has to be default-deny. The installed schema has more ways to act than click, type, fill, select and press: `batch` (a list of nested actions), `clickCoords`, `drag` and `hover`; an act can also arrive inside a nested `request` object; `open` takes `targetUrl` where other actions take `url`; `node` and `dashboard` choose a browser without naming a profile. A hook that checks only `kind`, `url` and `profile`, as first written, can be walked around.
The tool's schema can change with any OpenClaw update. Default-deny keeps a new action blocked until someone allows it, but the hook's eval cases still have to be rerun in each weekly patch window.

An approval prompt that shows the site and a field count does not tell the approver what is being sent; one that shows the values puts a child's details on the approval surface, which the docs advise against. Approval is a brake on mistakes, not a defence against exfiltration.
On iMessage the documented text fallback treats a Like tapback as allow-once. A reflex tapback on the prompt is an approval.
The approval branch has one consumer in the roadmap, the M6 jobs agent. Build and test it there, not in this batch.
corrections.safety: This is what turns 'the model was told not to' into a limit the model cannot argue past: profile, site and action limits live in code and fail closed, in line with both vendors' guidance to restrict sites and confirm consequential actions. It does not by itself make a logged-in browser safe (see WEB-04). It is in-house code sitting on the security boundary: one parsing mistake is a bypass, so it needs its own injection eval cases before any profile on the host holds a login.

Whether tapback approval works in iMessage Basic mode; the typed /approve command is the documented fallback.
The parameter names were read from the browser tool's schema source, not observed in a live hook event.

Whether the hook sees the browser call before the tool applies its own defaults (profile, target), so that 'must be present' can be enforced.
corrections.example: Trigger: an injected page tells the research agent to switch to another browser profile or to type into a form; the call is refused in code before the browser sees it, and the nightly eval has a case for each.
corrections.description: One in-house plugin that decides in code what each agent's browser may do: which profile, which sites and which actions, all as allowlists that fail closed. Without it the browser tool is all-or-nothing. In this batch it only denies; asking a parent before typing is a later addition for the M6 jobs agent.

Recommended path, available once F019, F007 and F067 exist (none is built; today's tools are web_search and home_weather only):

-main builds the copy-paste block from vault facts (F067); research confirms the opening time and the direct link with web_fetch (F026, F029); `automations` sets the reminder (F007); the parent fills the form with browser autofill and submits. Not-recommended path, for the record: a `

-forms` agent with `browser` on a managed profile, the WEB-03 hook with an exact registration-host allowlist, `fill` and `select` behind `requireApproval`, `type` with `submit` and `press` blocked, and the parent finishing over Screen Sharing.
caveats: The form ends in a booking and usually a payment, both on the never list, so the agent would stop exactly where the time pressure is.
The browser lives on the Mac mini in the happy account. 'Finish it yourself' means Screen Sharing into that session from a phone, which is slower than filling the form on the phone.
A large registration platform's terms forbid robots and automated registration processing; expect waiting rooms and bot checks on popular sign-ups.

The form needs a child's name, birth date, health notes and emergency contacts. An agent that holds those and reads an arbitrary web page has all three trifecta legs, and vendor guidance treats typing sensitive data into a form as transmitting it.
Web agents are measurably unreliable on live sites; a mis-click on a timed registration costs the slot.
Browser autofill already stores names, addresses and contact details and fills them in one tap.
The substitute card is a use of F067, F029 and F007, not a new feature, and it cannot be assembled until the research agent, reminders and the vault exist.

The autofill page read lists contact details, addresses, payment methods and passwords. A child's birth date, health notes and emergency contacts are not on that list, so those fields still come from the copy-paste block and are typed by the parent.

The copy-paste block sends a child's health notes and emergency contacts through the cloud model and into an iMessage thread. That is the existing F067 decision, not a new one, but it is the sensitive part of this feature.

corrections.how: Mechanism choice: an email already sent by the service. One-time parent step in the lunch portal: enable the low-balance email for each student and set the amount; then get those messages into the school mailbox (F051): a forwarding rule in the parent's own mail if it survives the mailbox's sender check, otherwise the parent forwards the alert by hand. The lunch account's login email stays the parent's. Reader: the tool-less, memory-less `school-mail` agent with the sender on its allowlist; the line is rendered by the F056 digest job. No web_fetch, no browser, no API. Topping up stays with the parent.
caveats: You hear about it only when the balance crosses the threshold. "What is the balance right now" needs a login and belongs to the parent's app.
One vendor documents a small fixed number of emails per low-balance episode, so a broken forwarding rule means silence. Test the rule once with a high threshold.
Balance pages sit next to stored payment methods, so a logged-in browser on this portal is not recommended even read-only (WEB-04 exclusion).
The service's app can already notify the phone; the gain is one digest instead of another app to check.
The parent already receives this email in their own inbox. The feature only repeats it as a digest line.

The cited service also offers AutoPay, an automatic top-up at a low-balance threshold. A family that turns it on never needs this alert. Turning it on is a payment set-up for the parent alone; Happy takes no part.

Forwarding has two traps. The mailbox plugin passes mail to the reader only when local verification finds an aligned DMARC pass for the allowlisted sender, and auto-forwarded mail can fail that; test with one real alert. And do not solve it by moving the lunch account's login email to the school mailbox: password-reset mail for an account with stored payment methods would then land in a mailbox an agent reads.
unverified: Which lunch payment system the district uses and whether it offers the same alert; the cited service is one example.
No parent-facing balance API was found for the cited service; absence is not proven.
Whether a filter-forward of this vendor's alert from the parent's mail passes the mailbox plugin's sender check.

corrections.how: A decision record plus two config guards: leave `tools.web.fetch.provider` unset and do not install `@openclaw/firecrawl-plugin` (once selected, its fetch fallback works without a key); add no remote CDP profile for a hosted browser. Agent instructions for research and any portal agent: on a login wall, CAPTCHA, MFA prompt or a 403, stop and report the exact blocker, which is what the bundled browser skill already tells the agent to do. caveats: CAPTCHA solving is on the family's never list, and a model vendor's own browser agent is barred from bypassing captchas.
A hosted browser or fetch proxy sees every URL and page: a new third party for family traffic.
The docs warn that automated logins trip anti-bot defenses and can lock the account; a locked school or library account costs more than any feature here is worth.
Getting around a site's bot controls can breach its terms of use.
The price of saying no: stock checks and some rec-department pages will come back as 'could not verify'.

Absence is the control, so it has to be checked: a second door exists in the summarize CLI's own fallback switch, and a future plugin install or stray API key would open the first one again. Add 'no fetch provider, no hosted browser profile' to the deploy drift check.
